cards.text: King Josiah of Judah just heard the Book of the Law read, and he tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). The prophetess Huldah said the LORD would bring calamity on this place, but Josiah's eyes would not see it (2 Kings 22:16, 20). Then the king summons all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

cards.question: Josiah goes up to the house of the LORD. Who goes up there with him?

answers.text: All the people small and great
Only the elders and the priests

cards.question: In the hearing of everyone, Josiah ___ all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.

cards.text: The KING reads it. Out loud. ALL the words, with no skimming and no “you can finish the rest at home, folks.”

cards.question: Then Josiah stands by the pillar before the LORD. What does he make there?

answers.text: A covenant to follow the LORD
A plan to rebuild the city walls
A vow to never go to war

cards.question: Josiah makes this covenant alone, and the people stay out of it.

cards.text: Everybody's in. Then Josiah gives orders to Hilkiah the high priest, the priests second in rank and the doorkeepers.

cards.question: What does Josiah order Hilkiah and the priests to remove from the temple of the LORD?

answers.text: The articles made for Baal and Asherah
The old stones from the repair work

cards.text: He burns them outside Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron and carries their ashes to Bethel. Friend, I spent YEARS in a junk drawer nobody ever cleaned out, and this man is hauling off the ASHES.

cards.question: Josiah also does away with the priests the kings of Judah had ordained for the high places. What had those priests been doing?

answers.text: Burning incense to Baal and the sun

cards.text: Next up, the Asherah pole. Josiah brings it out of the house of the LORD, down to the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem.

cards.question: What does Josiah do to the Asherah pole in the Kidron Valley?

answers.text: Burns it and grinds it to powder
Buries it deep in the valley
Sends it back to its makers

cards.text: Then he throws its dust on the graves of the common people. Burned, POWDERED and scattered, that pole is not coming back for a sequel.

cards.question: Josiah also tears down the quarters of the male shrine prostitutes that were in the house of the LORD, where women had woven tapestries for Asherah.

cards.text: Then Josiah brings all the priests in from the cities of Judah.

cards.question: From Geba to Beersheba, Josiah ___ the high places where those priests had burned incense.

cards.text: He even tears down the high places at the entrance of the gate of Joshua, the governor of the city. Right there at the city gate, gone.

cards.question: The priests of the high places come up to the altar of the LORD in Jerusalem.

cards.text: They don't come up to the altar, but they do eat unleavened bread with their fellow priests.
Josiah keeps going, friend. Next he desecrates Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom.

cards.question: Why does Josiah desecrate Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom?

answers.text: So no one could sacrifice a child to Molech
So no army could camp in the valley
So no one could build houses there

cards.text: Then Josiah removes the horses the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, from the very entrance to the house of the LORD. Horses for the SUN at the LORD's front door is like a rival bakery's sign hanging over MY oven.

cards.question: Josiah keeps the chariots of the sun for his own army.

cards.text: The kings of Judah had set up altars on the roof near the upper chamber of Ahaz, a king of Judah before Josiah (2 Kings 16:1). And Manasseh, Josiah's grandfather, had set up altars in the two courtyards of the house of the LORD (2 Kings 21:18, 26).

cards.question: Josiah pulls down those altars, pulverizes them and throws their dust into the ___ Valley.

cards.text: Then he desecrates the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Corruption. They were built for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom, the abominations of the Sidonians, the Moabites and the Ammonites.

cards.question: Which king of Israel had built those high places for Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom?
At those high places, Josiah smashes the sacred pillars, cuts down the Asherah poles and covers the sites with human bones.

cards.text: Josiah even pulls down the altar at Bethel, the high place set up by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin, then burns the high place, grinds it to powder and burns the Asherah pole. Friend, that is not a quick wipe of the counter, that is a DEEP clean.

cards.question: At Bethel, Josiah turns and sees tombs on the hillside. What does he do with the bones inside them?

answers.text: Burns them on the altar to defile it
Moves them to a new grave

cards.text: It all happens according to the word of the LORD, through a man of God from Judah who cried out against this altar back in Jeroboam's day and said a son named Josiah would be born to the house of David (1 Kings 13:1-2). By NAME, friend, and I've been out of that drawer a long time and some mornings I STILL check my handle to make sure it says Dorin.
Then the king spots something and asks, “What is this monument I see?”

cards.question: Josiah asks about a monument at Bethel. Whose tomb do the men of the city say it is?

answers.text: The man of God who came from Judah

cards.question: Josiah orders the bones in the man of God's tomb burned on the altar too.

cards.text: “Let him rest,” said Josiah. “Do not let anyone disturb his bones.” So they leave his bones undisturbed, along with those of the prophet who had come from Samaria.

cards.question: Just as he did at Bethel, Josiah removes all the shrines of the high places in the cities of Samaria, set up by the kings of ___.

cards.text: On the altars he slaughters all the priests of the high places and burns human bones on them, then he returns to Jerusalem. Stick around, friend, because Josiah's story isn't done yet.

findings.problem: The right answer "All the people small and great" uses the passage's Bible-sounding phrasing. The two wrong answers are plain modern phrases built on "Only…", so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: This is a recap card. Card 3 already established that Josiah read all the words aloud in everyone's hearing, and this card adds nothing new from 2 Kings 23:2. It only restates that he reads it.
"where those priests had burned incense" points back to card 15, which is no longer on screen. The question doesn't say which priests.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "Josiah pulls down those altars" points back to card 5, which is no longer on screen. The question doesn't say which altars, such as the ones on the roof and in the two courtyards.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "At those high places" points back to card 7, which is no longer on screen. The statement doesn't say which high places, such as the ones east of Jerusalem that Solomon built.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The first sentence packs four actions into one card: he pulls down the altar at Bethel, burns the high place, grinds it to powder and burns the Asherah pole. The joke comes on top of that. This is more than two beats.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: This is Jeroboam's first appearance. The card gives only the text's description ("son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin") and never says simply who he is, such as Israel's king.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The joke's comparison doesn't share the fact's core action. The fact is a prophecy that named Josiah long before he was born. The comparison is Papa Dorin checking that his own handle still says Dorin. That isn't the same action, so it doesn't click right away. The run-on "and… and" sentence makes it harder to follow.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "the prophet who had come from Samaria" is a new person, and the card never says simply who he is.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Before the story-continues line, this card carries three events: he slaughters the priests on the altars, burns human bones on them and returns to Jerusalem. That is more than two beats.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is thin. Most story cards are flat retellings with no reaction or personality: stop 1 cards 7, 11, 15 and 19, and stop 2 cards 1, 5, 7 and 13. The few jokes are mild, like stop 1 card 13's "not coming back for a sequel" and stop 1 card 4's "no skimming." They read like a nice dad being pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
